newsitem.title: UK: Computer manufacturers bid to win more European customers.
newsitem.headline: Computer manufacturers bid to win more European customers.

text.p: Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Computer manufacturers are cutting prices in a bid to win more European customers but potential buyers remain to be convinced.
More than 40 percent of American households now own personal computers. In Europe the figure is less than 20 percent.

Most of the home computers in the United States can dial into the Internet, the world-wide network of computers linked by telephone lines. Less than four percent of Europeans are fully-fledged "Internauts".
This indifference to technology is held by some to be because Europeans fail to see the huge benefits that computer ownership can bring.
But others say Europeans' lack of enthusiasm reflects a hard-headed calculation of the advantages. The speed, reliability and utility currently available doesn't match the high cost of the equipment.

Subscribers to America Online Inc in the U.S. might soon find themselves in the European camp. Following a recruitment drive using nationwide television advertisements, would-be Internauts found it impossible to penetrate AOL's overworked computers for hours at a time.

Other subscribers to Internet services in the U.S. find telephone lines blocked as surfers sign on at the start of the day, and just keep the connection going. Local calls are often free in the U.S. so there is little incentive to log-off.
Europeans penetrating the Internet often find the content less than compelling, and rarely designed for their culture.
COMPAQ SEES PRICE CUTS BOOSTING PRIVATE SALES
COMPAQ Computer Corp the world's biggest personal computer maker and market leader in Europe, believs it can reignite European consumer interest with swingeing price cuts.

Next month COMPAQ will slash the price of its multimedia PCs to the equivalent of $1,400 before taxes from about $2,050. COMPAQ hopes this will stem the steady fall in sales growth to the home over the last two years.

Analysts are not sure this will have much of an impact, although as market leader, COMPAQ is likely to trigger at least matching price cuts from competitors like International Business Machines Corp, Hewlett-Packard and Siemens Nixdorf.

They say much bigger price cuts are needed for consumers to sit up and take notice. They speculate that the mass market for consumers will only be ignited by bigger cuts, and wonder if this new level of demand will be grabbed by new Asian manufacturers turning televisions into computers.
COMPAQ'S Consumer Group vice-president Toon Bouten expects the price cuts to do the trick.

"The rates of growth in PC sales to the home market are in steep decline, while there's been a steady increase in price. We need multimedia PCs at lower prices; that will get greater penetration in the market for us," Bouten said in an interview.
"At the end of this month we will announce a $1,400 full multimedia PC, and that's how we want to get an additional boost to the market from first time buyers."
COMPAQ's current entry-level multimedia PC costs $2,054. Multimedia PCs include word-processing, video, sound, fax, Internet communications and graphics.
Bouten said European computer sales lagged because disposable incomes were 25 percent lower than in the U.S, and prices 10 percent higher.
"Europeans earn less and pay more. This is hampering (PC) growth in Europe."
ANALYSTS DOUBT PRICE CUT IMPACT
Fiona Macrae, market analyst with U.S. high technology consultantcy IDC, expects sales to increase with this price cut, but not by much.

"The German economy (Europe's biggest) is still in a total mess and austerity measures look set to continue. It (a PC) is still an awful lot of money; it's a step in the right direction but it won't trigger a mass market," she said.
Chris Herbert, PC analyst at market researcher Romtec, also doubts whether these price cuts will set off any big buying sprees.
"The consumer market is more difficult to capture (than business). $1,400 may be substantially lower, but will it be low enough to entice the next level of consumers?" Herbert said.
"Network computers, and a new Sony PC priced at around 400 to 500 quid ($600 to $750); that's a massive drop. That will capture a lot of people I think," Herbert said.
ASIANS, JAPANESE MAY WIN MASS MARKET
And that is the worry for mainstream computer makers, mainly American or European.

Japanese and Asian high-technology providers have so far made little impact on the world of computers, but they may have the key to assail the computer mass market from their experience in computer games and television, and their understanding of what consumers want and how to sell it to them.
PCTV OR TVPC?
"Will people go for a PCTV or TVPC?" said Emmanuel Lalloz, analyst with computer market researcher CONTEXT.

Experts have speculated that there could be two routes to the mass use of computers. One envisages computers eventually being able to include a TV facility, the other approach sees TVs gradually gaining the power to offer computing as well, like WebTV now being sold in the U.S.
"It is still not clear what the industry wants and what people want; fragmentation is rampant," Lalloz said.

"Now Sony and TV manufacturers are getting in as well, and they've got a lot of strength. Most of them are big manufacturers and if they require RAM or chips (computer building blocks) they can introduce into the system," said Lalloz.
"These people know the retail channel and the consumer market. PC multimedia for consumers? There's not a vast difference in marketing," Lalloz said.
